title: Ingress traffic shaping and source IP preservation — notes & terraform changes
body:
Purpose:
This note is a working draft for (1) preserving client source IPs through our ingress stack on private deployments (VPC and on-prem edge) and (2) shaping/limiting ingress traffic at the border (L4/L7) before it reaches internal services. Focus is practical: terraform changes, smoke tests, observability hooks, and rollback guidance.

Context and motivation:
- Customers running Redwood Private often require source IP visibility for auditing, rate-limiting, geo-routing, or external WAF integration.
- Default LB/proxy configurations in on-prem and some cloud setups terminate client IP and replace it with proxy IP (loss of client context).
- We need to document an interoperable approach across (a) cloud load balancers + autoscaled nodepools and (b) on-prem edge with hardware load balancers or metal proxies.
- Additionally, we want to apply coarse ingress shaping (per-VIP or per-route) to protect control-plane endpoints and to implement a graceful admission policy during bursts.

Assumptions (explicit):
- Customer clusters use either k8s with nodePort/Ingress or a VM-based service layer behind a perimeter LB.
- We can modify terraform modules for both cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) and generic on-prem (metal LB, HAProxy/NGINX) interfaces.
- Customers are OK with brief maintenance windows for rolling kernel/proxy config changes when necessary.

High-level approach options (pros/cons):
1) Preserve via proxy-protocol / X-Forwarded-For passthrough
   - Cloud LB: enable proxy protocol (or use preserved-source-ip option when using NLB/IP target) + configure target to trust proxy header.
   - On-prem: enable PROXY protocol on metal LB or use direct routing (DSR).
   - Pros: minimal app changes when apps already honor XFF.
   - Cons: intermediate proxies need to be configured/trusted; header spoofing risk if misconfigured.

2) Preserve via source IP preservation (route 1:1 NAT / preserve source)
   - Use SR-IOV/secondary interfaces or NAT rules that preserve client source for pod-to-pod ingress.
   - Pros: true source IP at socket level.
   - Cons: more complex network config, possible scaling limits (conntracking), not always supported in managed LB.

3) Sidecar-aware approach (for k8s): envoy/ingress with PROXY + original_src
   - Envoy can be configured to read PROXY/XFF and set original_src connection metadata for policies and telemetry.

Terraform module changes (notes to implement):
- Module: modules/lb/aws-nlb (cloud)
  * add variable: enable_proxy_protocol (bool, default false)
  * add variable: preserve_client_ip_mode (string enum: "none","proxy_protocol","ip_preserve")
  * when preserve_client_ip_mode=="proxy_protocol" -> enable proxy_protocol attribute on target group / listeners
  * when preserve_client_ip_mode=="ip_preserve" -> documented as experimental, requires doc + preflight checks (VPC route table, nodePort config)

- Module: modules/lb/generic-metal
  * add template snippets for HAProxy/NGINX to accept PROXY protocol or forward XFF unchanged
  * add config toggle: enable_proxy_protocol and proxy_protocol_version
  * add hook to push config and reload with zero-downtime (haproxy reload + config diff checks)

- Module: modules/k8s/ingress-controller
  * expose controller args: --use-proxy-protocol, --forwarded-for-header, --set-real-ip-from (list CIDR)
  * add note: when enabling proxy_protocol, set service.externalTrafficPolicy = Local to preserve source IP in k8s -> update terraform charts accordingly

- Module: modules/network/nat-gateway
  * expose conntrack_size and tcpmss_adjust parameters for on-prem NAT devices
  * add variable: nat_session_timeout_override for customers migrating from legacy NAT timeouts (note: affects long-lived connections)

Concrete firewall rules (examples to include in terraform vars / security groups):
- control-plane ingress (management plane): allow tcp 443 from management-proxies CIDR only
- customer-vip: allow 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (or restricted CIDR) but rate-limit at LB level to 500 rps burst 1000
- health-checks: allow LB health CIDRs (cloud) and on-prem monitoring CIDRs
- ssh/jumpbox: allow 22 from admin-office CIDR only

Ingress shaping primitives (implementation sketches):
- At LB: native rate-limiting (Nginx/haproxy) per-vhost with burst + token-bucket; prefer to set in edge layer rather than in-controller.
- At ingress-controller: use EnvoyFilter to attach rate-limit service for fine-grained per-route limits.
- Node-level egress shaping (tc): to protect nodes from amplification when attackers spoof source; add tc qdisc rules via daemonset.

Kubernetes network policies guidance (for preserved source IP use-cases):
- When external traffic policy = Local, source IPs will be actual client IPs; network policies should match on ipBlock/CIDR where appropriate.
- If using proxy/XFF only, policies must continue matching on pod selectors and rely on proxy ACLs for client allowlist.

Testing / verification matrix (must run in staging):
1) Proxy protocol path
   - configure LB to send PROXY v2 -> confirm ingress controller logs show PROXY handshake and apps see XFF or preserved source via socket (ss/netstat).
   - verify header spoofing rejection by setting set-real-ip-from only to LB CIDRs.

2) IP preserve path
   - validate that tcpdump on the pod host shows client IP preserved to pod interface.
   - run integration test that asserts source IP is same as client from application logs.

3) Traffic shaping
   - synthetic load test: ramp to 2x expected baseline, assert LB rate-limit triggers and healthy fallback (503->429 mapping) not catastrophic.
   - ensure metrics exposed: ingress_rps, ingress_429, ingress_503, avg_latency_ms at edge.

Rollout / upgrade plan (stepwise):
- Phase 0: design review & customer pilot selection (small set of customers who need source IP).
- Phase 1: add terraform variables (feature-flag) + default off. Merge as non-breaking change.
- Phase 2: staged deploy to staging clusters; run verification matrix.
- Phase 3: opt-in pilot customers enable preserve_client_ip_mode. Monitor for 72h.
- Phase 4: broaden rollout with runbook and optional infra changes (conntrack increases).
- Rollback: flip terraform var back to previous mode (e.g., disable proxy_protocol) and restore LB config; for on-prem, push previous HAProxy conf and reload.

Operational playbook snippets (for runbook):
- Preflight checklist: curl LB health endpoints, confirm LB CIDR blocks, backup current LB config, estimate conntrack usage via netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED | wc -l.
- During migration: schedule maintenance window for customers with long-lived TCP streams (websockets).
- Post-migration checks: spot check application logs for client_ip fields, check WAF integrations, confirm rate-limits still enforced.

Open questions / risks (to resolve before wide rollout):
- conntrack exhaustion on on-prem NAT devices for high-connection workloads (threat: session churn causes pod to hit conntrack limits). Mitigation: increase conntrack table, use eBPF socket attach for bypass.
- header spoofing risk if set-real-ip-from not tightened; need automated verification test.
- HD/legacy LB devices in some customers may not support PROXY -> require custom path/migration playbook.

Back-of-envelope terraform code snippets (notes for devs):
- aws nlb listener resource: set proxy_protocol_policy and attach to target group when enable_proxy_protocol = true
- ingress-controller helm values: server.extraArgs: ["--use-proxy-protocol=true", "--set-real-ip-from=10.0.0.0/8"]
- haproxy template: bind *:443 accept-proxy

Monitoring & alerts to add (minimum):
- Alert ING-01: ingress_429 > 5% of requests sustained for 5m (investigate rate-limit misconfig).
- Alert ING-02: abnormal change in client IP distribution (e.g., sudden 100% from one CIDR) -> possible header spoofing.
- Dashboard panels: per-VIP rps, per-VIP client_ip-cardinality, top client CIDRs, LB error rates, conntrack usage.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands
- tcpdump on node: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <client-ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/cap.pcap
- validate PROXY on envoys: curl -sS --http0.9 http://localhost:15000/config_dump | grep PROXY
- check k8s service config: kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml | yq '.spec.externalTrafficPolicy'

Next actions (owner assigned):
- (Aisha) create PR with terraform variable stubs for modules/lb/aws-nlb and modules/lb/generic-metal. Target: 2026-03-05.
- (Connor) write staging test plan and k8s manifest examples for proxy protocol. Target: 2026-03-08.
- (Sofia) gather a list of pilot customers and identify on-prem LB models that are in-field. Target: 2026-03-10.
- (Jamal) prepare monitoring dashboards and alert runbook. Target: 2026-03-12.

Notes-to-self (short):
- Keep default behavior off: do not flip preserve on by default.
- Document explicit customer opt-in and required preflight runbooks.
- Consider publishing a one-pager for customers summarizing implications for long-lived connections and WAFs.

End of draft.
